name: Child fever
tagline: When it is normal. When it is not.
sources: Red Cross War Memorial Children's Hospital

urgent.heading: See a clinic or hospital urgently if
urgent.primary_message: Most childhood fevers are not dangerous. But these signs change things — get to a clinic or hospital.
red_flags: Baby under 3 months with any fever (38°C or higher)
Fever over 40°C in a child of any age
Rash that doesn't fade when pressed under a glass
Stiff neck, severe headache, or sensitivity to light
Drowsy, hard to wake, or unusually quiet
Persistent vomiting or no urine for 8+ hours
Seizures — even brief ones need assessment

what_is_it.heading: Fever in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Fever is a body temperature over 38°C. It is not a disease — it is the body's way of fighting infection. Most childhood fevers are useful and not dangerous in themselves.
paragraphs: Fever helps the immune system work harder against viruses and bacteria. The temperature itself rarely causes harm in a child — even a high temperature is not 'frying' the brain (this is a common worry but not how fever damages bodies). What matters is what's causing it and how the child looks.

A child with a normal-feeling 39°C can be much less worrying than a child with 38°C who is floppy, refusing to feed, or unusual in any way. Trust how the child looks more than the thermometer. When in doubt, get them checked.

items.headline: Mostly OK
items.body: Most childhood fevers are viral, last 2–3 days, and resolve without treatment. The fever itself is rarely the problem.

items.headline: Under 3 months
items.body: Babies under 3 months with any fever need urgent medical assessment. Their immune systems are immature and infections can be serious.

items.headline: Watch the child
items.body: How the child looks and acts matters more than the number on the thermometer. A bright child with a high fever is less worrying than a floppy one with a mild fever.

items.headline: No antibiotics
items.body: Antibiotics don't treat viruses. Most childhood fevers are viral — antibiotics won't help and can cause side effects.

pull_quote.text: Don't chase the thermometer. Look at your child. A child who is interactive, drinking, and producing wet nappies is doing well — even with a high fever. A floppy, glassy-eyed child needs help — even with a mild fever.
pull_quote.source: Red Cross War Memorial Children's Hospital

signs.heading: How to tell if it's serious
signs.lede: Fever in itself isn't the danger. Look at the whole picture — your child's behaviour, breathing, fluids, and any other symptoms.

items.title: Probably OK
items.description: Child is interactive (playing, smiling, watching), drinking fluids, producing wet nappies, no rash, no breathing difficulty. Fever can be high but the child looks like themselves.

items.title: Watch closely
items.description: Child unusually quiet, less playful than normal, slightly off feeds, fever lasting 24–48 hours, mild rash. Not emergency but worth a clinic visit if it persists or worsens.

items.title: Get help now
items.description: Floppy or unresponsive, breathing fast or with effort, rash that doesn't fade under glass, stiff neck, refusing all fluids, no urine for 8+ hours, seizures, or any baby under 3 months with any fever.

items.title: Dress lightly — keep the room comfortable
items.description: Light clothing, light blanket if shivering. Don't bundle in heavy blankets or wrap up — this raises body temperature further.

items.title: Offer fluids often
items.description: Breastmilk, formula, water, ORS. Small amounts, often. Watch for wet nappies — a sign of good hydration.

items.title: Paracetamol or ibuprofen only for comfort
items.description: Not because of the number on the thermometer — only if the child seems uncomfortable. Follow weight-based dosing on the bottle. Don't combine paracetamol and ibuprofen without medical advice.

items.title: Don't sponge with cold water or alcohol
items.description: This is uncomfortable and can cause shivering, which raises temperature. Lukewarm water is fine if the child wants it.

items.title: Trust your instinct
items.description: If something feels wrong — even if you can't say what — go to a clinic. Parents pick up on subtle changes that matter. Healthcare workers prefer you bring a child for nothing than miss something.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Most childhood fevers can be managed at home. Knowing when to escalate is the key skill — and clinics are happy to see worried parents.
